entries.title: AI, JD, and other letters of the law
entries.summary: Ryan chats with Kevin Frazier, director of the AI Innovation and Law program at the University of Texas School of Law, about the legal and social impacts of data centers, the realities of workforce disruption, and regulating AI for child safety using existing consumer protection laws.
entries.content:
Ryan chats with Kevin Frazier, director of the AI Innovation and Law program at the University of Texas School of Law, about the legal and social impacts of data centers, the realities of workforce disruption, and regulating AI for child safety using existing consumer protection laws.

The AI Innovation and Law program at the University of Texas School of Law explores the complex legal and policy questions surrounding artificial intelligence, which Kevin also covers on his own podcast, Scaling Laws.

entries.title: AI cybersecurity is a cat and mouse game
entries.summary: Ryan chats with Sam Curry, CSO at Zscaler, about where human intelligence sits in the new security landscape with AI, why shifting security protections closer to applications helps limit probes for vulnerabilities, and why building more resilient code infrastructure is the best way to address the vulnerabilities AI does discover.
entries.content:
Ryan chats with Sam Curry, CSO at Zscaler, about where human intelligence sits in the new security landscape with AI, why shifting security protections closer to applications helps limit probes for vulnerabilities, and why building more resilient code infrastructure is the best way to address the vulnerabilities AI does discover.

Zscaler is a cybersecurity company that provides cloud-based security solutions, zero trust architecture, and TLS inspection to help organizations securely operate in multi-tenant environments.

entries.title: (Re)introducing Developer Story
entries.summary: For the past few years, we’ve been looking at ways to bring a little more of the individual developer back to Stack.
entries.content:
I won’t bury the good news here: Stack Overflow is bringing back the Developer Story.

Time for a short history lesson: once upon a time, we had a feature called Developer Story (“Dev Story”)—think of it as a resume or a CV on steroids. It tracked a developer’s career, added inflection points such as new jobs or languages learned, and was generally an all-around useful function to have.

Then, about five years ago, we deprecated this much-loved feature. Many of the most dedicated developers on the site (and on the internet!) expressed their frustration with that choice.

For the past few years, we’ve been looking at ways to bring a little more of the individual developer back to Stack. In short, we've done a great job showcasing your knowledge, but not the people creating that knowledge.

Dev Story is how we fix that.

Why now?

We realize that people don’t need to come directly to Stack Overflow anymore in order to get answers to their programming questions—the chatbots have that covered. Most LLMs have been trained on our datasets, providing a quick interface to our answers.

But we believe creators should derive value from their work.

And that’s where Dev Story comes in.

What’s new?

It’s a smarter tool built to showcase your true expertise.

Right now, on day 1, we’re supporting what we’re calling “specialties”—these are areas where you have proven expertise, distilled and pulled forward for everyone to see. But we also give you the control over which specialties are highlighted.

Soon, we will also display and report out your non-SO contributions (from integrations with other sites that have verified data about you, as well as from other sites in our own network).

And we’re building it in a privacy-centric way—we won’t be displaying any private info that you don’t EXPLICITLY tell us to display.

And the part that truly excites me: Dev Story will be at the heart of your profile on Stack Overflow, acting as a much fuller picture of your technical identity.

And then there’s Stack Identity

Dev Story is the foundation of an even broader vision.

This suite of tools is what we’re referring to as “Stack Identity”. It will be the verified developer proof-of-work layer to the internet.

The core concept: your technical contributions should speak for themselves.

You will use Stack Identity to prove and showcase your skills and career. Anyone can list languages on a CV, but your work here, and in places that work with Stack Identity, reveal your true expertise.

Stack Overflow is uniquely suited to deliver this level of verification.

Go try it

But for now, go check out the Dev Story. It showcases your contributions to the site, who you’ve helped, and how long you’ve been plugging away.

There are places for you to add items to your timeline, to edit your specialties, and more.

One note: your old Dev Story will not be there. Unfortunately, the data for that met the old 

rm -rf
treatment when we discontinued it last time for privacy compliance reasons. We brought the concept back, but we can't 
sudo undelete
the past.

I will caveat this with: this is a “release early and often” feature for us. Our team is making changes on a daily basis and pushing things out frequently. Look for improvements to the specialties tool, integrations with other sites, and new ways to demonstrate expertise.

This is about highlighting YOUR expertise.

So check it out, play with the settings, tell us what you think, and send us your feature ideas!

We're building this platform around the developer community, and we want you involved every step of the way.
